Recently, I worked on a project comparing Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, with Context Augmented Generation to see how different ways of giving an LLM information can affect its answers.

For the project, I used a single document as the main source of information and tested different ways of getting that information into the model. With RAG, the document was split into smaller chunks and the system searched for the chunks that were most related to the question. With the other approach, more of the document was placed directly into the model's context.

I experimented with things such as chunk size and how many pieces of the document were retrieved for each question. I also had to think about the tradeoff between giving the model more information and using more context than was actually needed.

What interested me most was seeing how much the setup around the model can affect the final response. Using the same language model does not always mean getting the same quality of answer. The way information is stored, searched, and passed into the model can make a large difference.

This project gave me more experience working with LLMs, embeddings, vector search, and evaluating generated responses. It also helped me understand RAG beyond just knowing the definition and gave me a better idea of when it could actually be useful in a larger application.
